Chapter 16, Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga, the Yoga of the Division between the Divine and Demonic Endowments, continues without any question from Arjuna, moving from chapter 15's vision of the Supreme Person to a stark moral portrait of two kinds of created beings. Kṛṣṇa opens with two matching catalogs: the divine endowment (daivī sampad) — fearlessness, purity of being, self-control, non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion, gentleness, patience, and more — and, set directly against it, the demonic endowment (āsurī sampad) — hypocrisy, pride, self-conceit, anger, harshness, ignorance. The one leads to liberation, the other to bondage, and Kṛṣṇa reassures Arjuna that he himself was born with the divine nature. The chapter then turns, at length, to portray the demonic mind from the inside: those who hold the world to be godless and without foundation, produced by nothing but the chance union of male and female and driven by desire alone; who chase insatiable appetite, hoard wealth by unjust means, and rehearse to themselves a boastful inner monologue — "this I have gained, this I shall gain next, I am the lord, I am accomplished, who is there like me?" — even as they perform sacrifice only in name, out of hypocrisy and without regard for scriptural rule, and hate the divine presence in their own bodies and in others'. Such men, Kṛṣṇa says, he hurls again and again into demonic wombs, sinking further from him birth after birth. The chapter closes by naming the threefold gate of hell that destroys the self — desire, anger, and greed — urging their abandonment, and ends with a plain statement of the poem's governing principle: whoever discards the authority of scripture and acts on mere desire attains neither success, nor happiness, nor the highest goal, so that scripture must be the standard by which one determines what should and should not be done.
